habitat: Caribbean flamingos, also known as American flamingos, inhabit coastal lagoons, mudflats, mangrove swamps, and shallow saline lakes across the Caribbean Basin — from the Bahamas, Cuba, and Hispaniola through the Yucatan Peninsula to coastal Venezuela and Colombia, with a small population in the Galapagos Islands. They require alkaline or saline shallow water bodies with abundant algae and invertebrates for feeding. Nesting colonies are established on isolated mud islands, sandbars, and salt flats that offer protection from terrestrial predators.
diet: Caribbean flamingos are filter feeders, consuming algae (particularly Spirulina), diatoms, small crustaceans (brine shrimp), mollusks, and aquatic insects. Their iconic pink coloration comes from carotenoid pigments in their food — primarily from Spirulina algae and brine shrimp. Flamingos feed by submerging their head upside-down and sweeping it through the water, using their uniquely structured beak and tongue to filter food particles. They may consume up to 60 grams of food per day, requiring extensive feeding areas.
behavior: Caribbean flamingos are among the most social of all birds, living in colonies from dozens to tens of thousands. Their courtship is spectacular — synchronized group displays involving head-flagging, wing-salutes, twist-preens, and marching, with hundreds of birds performing simultaneously. Pairs are seasonally monogamous, jointly building mud nests and incubating a single egg for 27-31 days. Both parents produce 'crop milk' — a nutritious secretion from their upper digestive tract — to feed the chick. Chicks form large crèches (nursery groups) while parents forage.
facts: The Caribbean flamingo is the brightest and largest flamingo species, the only one naturally occurring in North America. Their pink color intensifies with diet — zoo flamingos may fade without carotenoid-rich food. They can live 40-50 years, among the longest-lived birds. Flamingos stand on one leg to conserve body heat and reduce muscle fatigue. Their knee is actually their ankle — what appears to be a backward-bending knee is the bird's equivalent of a heel. The word 'flamingo' comes from the Spanish 'flamenco,' referencing their flame-colored plumage.
naming: Flamingo names might reflect their pink color, elegant stance, or tropical habitat. Consider names like Coral, Pinky, Flamingle, Rose, Laguna, Sunset, Hibiscus, Salsa, Flamenco, or Mai Tai.
